Vikas: Lalit Chacha, both families keep arguing about the rituals and the guest numbers. We'd like you to hear each side and tell us what they want.
Lalit: Why me?
Kritika: Because both families respect you, and you'll be fair.
Lalit: All right. I'll see your parents first, then Vikas's. I'll only ask two things: what matters most, and what can bend.
Vikas: Thank you. We'll keep the guest number flexible.
Lalit: (a week later) Kritika's mother wants the haldi with all the relatives. Vikas's father wants fewer than two hundred guests. What if haldi is for the close family, and the reception is the big one?
Kritika: That could work.
Vikas: I'll tell my parents.
Lalit: No, I'll tell both sets together, so nobody thinks the other side got more.

Our families spent a whole month arguing before Ritika and I tried something different.
Her side wanted the full three-day set of rituals. Mine wanted one day and a larger guest list. Every phone call ended with someone's mother in tears, and Ritika and I stuck in the middle.
Then Ritika said, "What about Omkar mama?" He's her mother's brother, but my father respects him too; they played cricket together as boys. Everyone listens when he talks.
We went to his house with a list. He agreed to carry messages both ways. For two weeks he visited each family, listened, and came back with what each side really cared about. Her side mainly wanted the haldi and the pheras done properly. Mine mainly cared about inviting the village.
The final plan: two days, both rituals, a big lunch. Nobody shouted once.
— Abhinav

qa.q: What did Ritika's side mainly want done properly?
How did Abhinav and Ritika feel before asking Omkar mama for help?
qa.a: They felt stuck and strained, caught in the middle of phone calls that ended in tears.

qa.q: Which other approach could the couple have tried alongside the uncle's help?
qa.a: They could first write their own shared values for the wedding, so they knew which compromises they would accept before the uncle carried messages.

qa.q: How might the two families have seen Omkar mama's visits?
qa.a: Both families likely felt listened to and respected, since a trusted person heard their real wishes instead of arguing on the phone.

grounding: It shows a couple asking a respected uncle to carry each family's wishes on rituals and guest numbers, so both feel respected and a compromise is reached with fewer fights.

Wedding planner's note, Lucknow — Imran and Farah's wedding

I've planned many weddings, and I want to record how this couple handled the families.
By our second meeting, the two sides disagreed on almost everything. Imran's family wanted a nikah and a separate walima for four hundred guests. Farah's family wanted one combined event and a smaller list.
Imran and Farah didn't argue at my table. Instead they asked Samir chacha, Imran's father's elder brother, whom Farah's parents also admired, to go between the two houses.
Over ten days he visited each family twice. He came back to my office with a short list: Imran's side mostly cared about the walima; Farah's side mostly cared about keeping the numbers modest.
The compromise: nikah at home, a walima for two hundred. Both mothers hugged at the final meeting.
My next step: I've asked Samir chacha if I can call him for the seating plan.

qa.q: How many guests were invited to the walima in the final compromise?
How might Imran and Farah have felt when both mothers hugged at the final meeting?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and happy, seeing that the families felt respected after weeks of disagreement.

qa.q: What else could the couple have done if Samir chacha had not been available?
qa.a: They could have met with both families together with simple ground rules and one request from each side.

qa.q: How did the arrangement look to Farah's family?
qa.a: Farah's family felt respected, since their wish for modest numbers was carried by someone they admired and reflected in the final plan.

grounding: It shows a couple asking a respected uncle to relay each family's wishes on rituals and guests, so both families feel respected and a compromise is reached.
